ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> In each trial, participants were presented with the sentence "I think you are…" and a positive/negative word pair randomly selected from a list of 64 pairs (e.g., selfish vs. generous).

> At the end of each block, participants were asked to rate how much the persona liked them on a scale from 0 ('Dislike') to 100 ('Like').

> Immediately following the behavioral task, participants completed six self-report questionnaires selected a priori to assess their transdiagnostic relationship with social feedback learning, namely the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-10) (Allison et al., 2012), Social Phobia Inventory (SPIN) (Connor et al., 2000), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) (Beck et al., 1996), Apathy Motivation Index (AMI) (Ang et al., 2017), Narcissistic Admiration and Rivalry Questionnaire (NARQ) (Back et al., 2013), and Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) checklist (First et al., 1997).

> In the present task, however, there were no reversals and participants completed only 32 trials per condition block.

> An attention check was randomly assigned to two of the three blocks, where participants were asked to select a specific word: "Please select <word> to show you are paying attention...".

> Across all three blocks, participants were significantly more likely to choose the positive word than the negative word (Neutral: 73.1%, p < 0.001; Like: 74.6%, p < 0.001; Dislike: 68.9%, p < 0.001; Supplementary Figure 3), indicating a consistent initial bias towards the positive option across all conditions before any learning had taken place.

> The Social Evaluation Learning Task and behavioral results. (a) Participants were instructed to learn about the computer persona's perspective of themselves, which differs in the probability of positive/negative words being the correct choice.

> At the end of each block, participants were asked to provide a single rating on how much the persona disliked them using a Likert scale from 0 (Dislike) to 100 (Like).

Ethics approval statement:

> The authors assert that all procedures contributing to this work comply with the ethical standards of the relevant national and institutional committees on human experimentation and with the Helsinki Declaration of 1975, as revised in 2008.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p ≥ .115", "p-values < 0.05"), 
    Text = c("Trial exclusion rates were not significantly different across conditions ( 2 (2) = 5.87, p = 0.053), and was not significantly associated with any transdiagnostic factor score (all 𝜏 0.081, all p ≥ .115; Supplementary Table 1).", 
    "To evaluate model fit, we calculated Bayesian p-values as the proportion of predicted statistics more extreme than the corresponding observed statistic (two-tailed), with p-values < 0.05 indicating circumstances where the model fails to capture the observed data pattern."
    )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 139 columns across 3 data files.
#### Issues Identified

41 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: In each trial, participants were presented with the sentence "I think you are…" and a positive/negative word pair randomly selected from a list of 64 pairs (e.g., selfish vs. generous).
At the end of each block, participants were asked to rate how much the persona liked them on a scale from 0 ('Dislike') to 100 ('Like').

Immediately following the behavioral task, participants completed six self-report questionnaires selected a priori to assess their transdiagnostic relationship with social feedback learning, namely the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-10) (Allison et al., 2012), Social Phobia Inventory (SPIN) (Connor et al., 2000), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) (Beck et al., 1996), Apathy Motivation Index (AMI) (Ang et al., 2017), Narcissistic Admiration and Rivalry Questionnaire (NARQ) (Back et al., 2013), and Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) checklist (First et al., 1997).
In the present task, however, there were no reversals and participants completed only 32 trials per condition block.
An attention check was randomly assigned to two of the three blocks, where participants were asked to select a specific word: "Please select <word> to show you are paying attention...".

Across all three blocks, participants were significantly more likely to choose the positive word than the negative word (Neutral: 73.1%, p < 0.001; Like: 74.6%, p < 0.001; Dislike: 68.9%, p < 0.001; Supplementary Figure 3), indicating a consistent initial bias towards the positive option across all conditions before any learning had taken place.

The Social Evaluation Learning Task and behavioral results. (a) Participants were instructed to learn about the computer persona's perspective of themselves, which differs in the probability of positive/negative words being the correct choice.
At the end of each block, participants were asked to provide a single rating on how much the persona disliked them using a Likert scale from 0 (Dislike) to 100 (Like).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 17 R code files.
#### Run order

A dependency **cycle** was detected among 2 files (parameter_recovery.Rmd, simulation_recovery.Rmd): each reads a file another writes, so no run order satisfies all of them. This must be resolved before the code can run.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:15, File = c("behavioural_analysis.Rmd", 
"brms_coefficient_plots.R", "brms_config.R", "brms_collate.R", 
"brms_regression_models.R", "build_dataList.R", "main_modelling_run_stan.R", 
"model_comparison.R", "modelling_analysis.Rmd", "positive_choice_analysis.R", 
"ppc.Rmd", "recovery_helpers.R", "restore_environment.R", "run_models_array.R", 
"simulation_ppc.Rmd"), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "behavioural_analysis.Rmd", 
"brms_config.R", "brms_config.R", "—", "—", "—", "behavioural_analysis.Rmd", 
"—", "behavioural_analysis.Rmd", "—", "—", "main_modelling_run_stan.R", 
"—"), Basis = c("none", "none", "dependency", "dependency", 
"dependency", "none", "none", "none", "dependency", "none", "dependency", 
"none", "none", "dependency", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -15L
), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **6 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Missing inputs
5 input files the code reads are in the deposit but not usable as named: too large to download, inside an archive, or under a similar name.

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("datalist.rdata", "data_exp_198741-v14_task-7y8x.csv",

# display table -----------------------------------

```
#### Files not run on their own
2 files only define functions, so running them on their own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 0 are used by no script in the deposit.

```{r}

table <- structure(list(File = c("recovery_helpers.R", "main_modelling_run_stan.R"
), "Used by" = c("parameter_recovery.Rmd, simulation_recovery.Rmd", 
"run_models_array.R")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 14 scripts: 3 ran without error, 9 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 2 were run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **2 scripts could not be tried, because a file they need was not downloaded**: modelling_analysis.Rmd, simulation_recovery.Rmd. They are not counted as scripts that did not reproduce. The files: social_feedback_learning_25_08_2026.zip/social_feedback_learning/stanfits/ws_rw_ppc.RData (203.1 MB), social_feedback_learning_25_08_2026.zip/social_feedback_learning/stanfits/ws_rw_rp_initV_shared_t1_ppc.RData (587.0 MB); files over 100 MB are not downloaded.

**`setwd()` in the code**

**3 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("brms_regression_models.R", "brms_collate.R", 
"run_models_array.R"), "setwd() removed" = c(1L, 1L, 1L), "Path(s) it set" = c("(non-literal)", 
"(non-literal)", "(non-literal)")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Other changes we made to run the code**

Stan files in the syntax Stan removed in version 2.33 were given the newer syntax, and Git LFS pointers (placeholders a GitHub archive holds instead of the file) were replaced by the deposit's copy of the file. Updating the Stan files, and depositing the files themselves, solves this.

```{r}
), Change = c("Stan from before 2.33: array declarations", "Stan from before 2.33: array declarations", 
"Stan from before 2.33: array declarations", "Stan from before 2.33: array declarations"
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

5 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

2 scripts are run by another script with `source()`, so they were not run on their own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on their own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Their outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

text.text: Learning from feedback provided by others is important for navigating complex social environments.
Aberrant processing of such social feedback is implicated in the psychopathology of several mental health disorders including social anxiety and depression.
Recent psychiatric research increasingly adopts transdiagnostic approaches that examine mechanisms and constructs cutting across traditional diagnostic categories.
Here, we applied reinforcement learning models together with transdiagnostic measures of psychopathology to formally assess social evaluation learning.
Human participants (n = 193) completed the Social Evaluation Learning Task, learning whether computer personas 'liked,' 'disliked,' or were 'neutral' toward them.
Participants also completed six questionnaires assessing socially relevant psychiatric traits.
Computational modeling revealed that a model with separate learning parameters for positive and negative feedback best accounted for the learning behavior.
Exploratory factor analysis identified three transdiagnostic factors.
A factor reflecting social avoidance predicted enhanced learning from negative feedback and a reduced positive learning bias.
Socially avoidant individuals with heightened negative learning rates additionally showed slower decision times specifically in positive social contexts.
A second factor linking with emotional insensitivity for others predicted a lower choice accuracy in both positively and negatively valenced conditions.
No significant associations emerged for a third factor reflecting depressive and mood-related symptoms.
These results demonstrate how transdiagnostic trait dimensions shape social learning mechanisms through specific behavioral and computational processes.
Learning from social feedback is a vital cognitive process enabling individuals to adjust their behavior based on social cues, such as praise and criticism (Bauer, 1967).
text.formatted: Learning from social feedback is a vital cognitive process enabling individuals to adjust their behavior based on social cues, such as praise and criticism <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bauer, 1967)</ref>.

text.text: This mechanism is crucial for navigating complex social environments, maintaining relationships, and shaping one's self-concept (Boyd et al., 2011; Button et al., 2012; Elder et al., 2022; FeldmanHall & Chang, 2018; Kendal & Watson, 2023; Olsson et al., 2020; Peters et al., 2024; Schröder et al., 2025).

text.text: In the form of social evaluative feedback, individuals update beliefs about the self and others (Behrens et al., 2008; Diaconescu et al., 2014) from external judgements or feedback which can differ in valence and expectancy (Peters et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In the form of social evaluative feedback, individuals update beliefs about the self and others <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Behrens et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Diaconescu et al., 2014)</ref> from external judgements or feedback which can differ in valence and expectancy <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Peters et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Social learning can be formally investigated using the framework of reinforcement learning (RL) (Sutton & Barto, 2018; Zhang & Gläscher, 2020), a form of error-based learning driven by differences between actual and expected outcomes (i.e., prediction error).
text.formatted: Social learning can be formally investigated using the framework of reinforcement learning (RL) <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Sutton & Barto, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zhang & Gläscher, 2020)</ref>, a form of error-based learning driven by differences between actual and expected outcomes (i.e., prediction error).

text.text: Application of the RL framework has revealed distinct biases in social feedback learning in several psychiatric disorders.
Yet, in the context of social feedback learning, existing research has primarily taken a categorical approach often focusing on a single disorder or trait.

For example, individuals with social anxiety (Beltzer et al., 2019 (Beltzer et al., , 2023;; Button et al., 2012; Hopkins et al., 2021; Koban et al., 2017 Koban et al., , 2023;; Müller-Pinzler et al., 2019; Zabag et al., 2022 Zabag et al., , 2024) ) and borderline personality disorder (Gregorová et al., 2024; Korn et al., 2016) are biased towards learning more strongly from negative social feedback, whilst depressed individuals conversely do not update their beliefs more strongly following positive compared to negative social feedback (Hobbs et al., 2022; Hoffmann et al., 2024).

text.text: Narcissistic traits bias perceptions toward evaluators that provide negative feedback about them (Kernis & Sun, 1994; Smalley & Stake, 1996), and individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) demonstrate lowered learning rates and accuracy when learning about others (Cahalan et al., 2026; Schuetze et al., 2017).

text.text: Additionally, the social dimension of apathy has recently been highlighted (Zhao et al., 2026), yet whether social learning is attenuated amongst apathetic individuals remains underexplored.

text.text: Compared to categorical assessments, a transdiagnostic approach to psychopathology (Gillan et al., 2016; Insel et al., 2010; Robbins et al., 2012; Tanaka, 2024) focuses on dimensional traits that cut across multiple disorders.

text.text: Latent psychological and cognitive constructs or factors of mental health can be extracted that more accurately map onto candidate cognitive processes (Gillan & Seow, 2020).

text.text: This approach can further be combined with the theorydriven computational modeling of behavior (Zhang, 2023; Sohail & Zhang, 2024), to infer the construct-specific computational processes that characterize a given factor (Wise et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This approach can further be combined with the theorydriven computational modeling of behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Zhang, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Sohail & Zhang, 2024)</ref>, to infer the construct-specific computational processes that characterize a given factor <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Wise et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Combining transdiagnostic assessments of psychopathology with computational models have identified the specific cognitive processes underlying altered behavior in mental health disorders, including model-based planning (Gillan et al., 2016), metacognition (Rouault et al., 2018), reward processing (Suzuki et al., 2021) and uncertainty (Norbury et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Combining transdiagnostic assessments of psychopathology with computational models have identified the specific cognitive processes underlying altered behavior in mental health disorders, including model-based planning <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Gillan et al., 2016)</ref>, metacognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Rouault et al., 2018)</ref>, reward processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Suzuki et al., 2021)</ref> and uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Norbury et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, a transdiagnostic account of how these traits may differentially influence learning from social feedback is currently not known.

To bridge these research gaps, we used the Social Evaluation Learning Task (SELT) (Button et al., 2012 (Button et al., , 2015)), a well-established paradigm to test participants' learning through valenced social feedback.
text.formatted: To bridge these research gaps, we used the Social Evaluation Learning Task (SELT) <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Button et al., 2012</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Button et al., , 2015))</ref>, a well-established paradigm to test participants' learning through valenced social feedback.

text.text: We adopted a transdiagnostic approach in a non-clinical sample, assessing relevant domains of psychopathology known to affect social behavior, including autism, social anxiety, depression, apathy, narcissism, and BDP.
We anticipated transdiagnostic factors reflecting social engagement and mood to be extracted from our questionnaire battery (Gillan et al., 2016; Oka et al., 2025; Schafer & Schiller, 2025).
text.formatted: We anticipated transdiagnostic factors reflecting social engagement and mood to be extracted from our questionnaire battery <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Gillan et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Oka et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Schafer & Schiller, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We also hypothesised these factors to differentially moderate social learning effects.

Specifically, we expected for social engagement to negatively correlate with a negative learning bias, and for a depressive-mood factor to positively correlate with reduced learning from positive feedback (Button et al., 2012; Hoffmann et al., 2024; Hopkins et al., 2021).

text.text: This study ultimately provides a nuanced understanding of how overlapping psychiatric traits relate to the ability to learn from social feedback. ticipants (Figure 1a).

text.text: Each persona followed a unique feedback contingency for the word pair: the positive word was the correct choice 80% of the time for the 'Like' persona, 20% for the 'Dislike' persona, and 50% for the 'Neutral' persona, whereas the negative word was the correct choice 20% of the time for the 'Like' persona, 80% for the 'Dislike' persona, and 50% for the 'Neutral' persona.
The feedback contingencies were not communicated to the participants; instead, participants needed to work these out using trial and error.
In each trial, participants were presented with the sentence "I think you are…" and a positive/negative word pair randomly selected from a list of 64 pairs (e.g., selfish vs. generous).
Participants firstly made a choice between the words, with no enforced time limit, followed by feedback on correctness (500ms) before a fixation cross (400ms).
Each block consisted of 32 trials, with the order of the three blocks randomized and counterbalanced across participants.
The placement of the two words on the screen was counterbalanced across trials, to avoid motor habituation.
At the end of each block, participants were asked to rate how much the persona liked them on a scale from 0 ('Dislike') to 100 ('Like').

Immediately following the behavioral task, participants completed six self-report questionnaires selected a priori to assess their transdiagnostic relationship with social feedback learning, namely the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-10) (Allison et al., 2012), Social Phobia Inventory (SPIN) (Connor et al., 2000), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) (Beck et al., 1996), Apathy Motivation Index (AMI) (Ang et al., 2017), Narcissistic Admiration and Rivalry Questionnaire (NARQ) (Back et al., 2013), and Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) checklist (First et al., 1997).

text.text: Three dependent variables were selected as indicators of task behavior: choice accuracy, decision time (DT), and end-of-block persona rating.
Choice accuracy was defined as selecting the word whose valence was associated with the feedback contingency; positive words for the 'Like' condition, negative words for the 'Dislike' condition.
For the neutral condition, there was no correct response.
We coded the 'Like' option as correct response ('Dislike' would reveal same results) to enable joint analysis of all conditions.
Raw untransformed DT were used for repeated-measures ANOVA, as subjectlevel mean DTs were normally distributed across all conditions (Shapiro-Wilk tests: W > 0.985; skewness = 0.09-0.24).
text.formatted: Raw untransformed DT were used for repeated-measures ANOVA, as subjectlevel mean DTs were normally distributed across all conditions (Shapiro-Wilk tests: W > 0.985; skewness = 0.09-0.24).

text.text: For trial-level mixed-effects models, we used log-transformed DT values.
The RL framework was applied to quantify the computational processes underlying task behavior.

Considering that participants may learn differently from positive versus negative social feedback (Zhang et al., 2020), we tested an RL model (against the simple Rescorla-Wagner model, Rescorla & Wagner, 1972) with two distinct learning rates (𝛼 + and 𝛼 -) for positive and negative prediction errors (PEs) -the difference between the received outcome (O, coded as -1 and 1) and the value (V, initialised at zero) for each trial (t):

text.text: The model space ultimately consisted of four models: single learning rate with no initialvalue bias, dual learning rate with no initial-value bias, single learning rate with initial-value bias, and dual learning rate with initial-value bias.
For the initial-value bias models, the softmax 𝛽 was not enforced on the first trial of each block for identifiability reasons.
Model estimation was conducted under the hierarchical Bayesian framework (Sohail & Zhang, 2025a) using the {rstan} (Carpenter et al., 2017), and {hBayesDM} (Ahn et al., 2017) R packages.

R-hat values for all parameters were below 1.02, indicating excellent model convergence (Gelman & Rubin, 1992).

text.text: Lower LOOIC scores signified superior model performance, and the model with the lowest LOOIC was chosen for further analyses.
An exploratory factor analysis was conducted to identify transdiagnostic factors across the six psychiatric questionnaires used.
To account for mixed item types (binary and ordinal), polychoric correlations were computed using the {polycor} package.
Factor analysis was performed using the 'fa' function from the {psych} package in R with maximum likelihood estimation and oblique (oblimin) rotation (Costello & Osborne, 2005).

text.text: Eighty of the eightytwo items (two removed due to zero-variance) across the six questionnaires were included.
A Cattell-Nelson-Gorsuch test was used through the {nFactors} package to determine the optimal number of factors.
Factor loadings ≥ 0.3 were deemed interpretable.
Factor scores were calculated using regression scoring weights and standardized for subsequent analyses.

To uncover transdiagnostic influences on behavioural and computational outcomes, we fit Bayesian mixed-effects regressions with transdiagnostic factor scores, task condition, and their interactions as predictors; a logistic (Bernoulli) model for choice accuracy, and Gaussian models for log-transformed DTs and end-of-block rating.
These analyses implemented the three-way model structure: with random intercepts and by-participant random slopes of condition.

Each computational parameter was modelled by task condition and factor scores: with random intercepts for each participant, for the positive learning rate (𝛼 + ), negative learning rate (𝛼 -), their difference (𝛼 + -𝛼 -), and inverse temperature (𝜏 ).

text.text: To determine whether participants exhibited asymmetric learning from positive versus negative feedback, we compared the four computational models crossing the learning-rate structure with the initial-value bias.

Model comparison revealed that the dual-learning-rate model with the shared initial-value bias provided the best overall fit, outperforming the next-best model (ΔLOOIC = 18.4; Supplementary Table 2), confirming that participants processed positive and negative social feedback differently.

text.text: Next, we tested whether learning rates varied as a function of feedback valence and persona condition.

A learning-rate valence (positive vs negative) by condition (Like, Dislike, Neutral) repeated-measures ANOVA (Greenhouse-Geisser corrected) revealed a significant main effect of learning-rate valence (F (1,192) = 465.51, p < 0.001) and condition (F~(1.27, 243.94)~= 52.27, p < 0.001), and a significant interaction (F~(1.27, 243.82)~= 111.26, p < 0.001), indicating that the relationship between feedback valence and learning varied across conditions (Figure 2a).

text.text: To examine whether individual differences in learning rates predicted behavioral performance, we ran Kendall's rank (𝜏 ) correlations between computational parameters and choice accuracy across conditions.

Both the positive learning rate (𝛼 + ; Kendall's 𝜏 = 0.262, p < 0.001) and the difference between the positive and negative learning rates -the positive learning bias -(𝛼 + -𝛼 -; Kendall's 𝜏 = 0.195, p < 0.001) were positively associated with accuracy in the 'Like' condition after Bonferroni correction (Figure 2b-c).

text.text: However, no significant relationship was observed for the negative learning rate (𝜏 = -0.055, p = 0.264).

As a follow-up analysis, we computed the mean trial-averaged learned value of the positiveword from the winning model (V positive ) and correlated it with participants' end-of-block ratings, to bridge computational learning signals with acquired social evaluations.

Kendall's 𝜏 correlations between mean V positive and ratings were significant in the Neutral (𝜏 = 0.161, z = 3.29, p = .001, r = 0.251) and Like (𝜏 = 0.235, z = 4.78, p < .001, r = 0.360) conditions, but not in the Dislike condition (𝜏 = 0.064, z = 1.30, p = .194, r = 0.10) (Figure 2d).

text.text: All these results highlight a direct link between the capacity to learn from social feedback and its recognition in social contexts reflected in task performance.

Our EFA analysis revealed that a 3-factor solution best accounted for the questionnaire data (25.8% of variances explained), identifying transdiagnostic dimensions of psychopathology that may relate to social feedback learning.

Based on the strongest individual item loadings (Figure 3), factors were labelled accordingly as 'Social Avoidance', with higher scores reflecting reduced social motivation and increased avoidance, 'Emotional Insensitivity', where higher scores indicate high apathy and difficulties evaluating and empathizing with others, and 'Depressive Self-Identity', where higher scores correspond to low mood, low self-esteem and negative self-identity.

text.text: To examine whether transdiagnostic factors predicted computational mechanisms underlying social feedback learning, we fit Bayesian mixed-effects models with computational parameters from the winning model as dependent variables (Figure 4a-c).
text.formatted: To examine whether transdiagnostic factors predicted computational mechanisms underlying social feedback learning, we fit Bayesian mixed-effects models with computational parameters from the winning model as dependent variables (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4a-c</ref>).

text.text: Condition effects on learning parameters were robust, with the Like condition credibly increasing positive learning rates (posterior mean = 0.075, 89% CrI [0.070, 0.081]) and decreasing negative learning rates (mean = -0.036, 89% CrI [-0.047, -0.026]), while the Dislike condition credibly increased both positive learning rates (mean = 0.067, 89% CrI [0.062, 0.073]) and positive learning bias (mean = 0.060, 89% CrI [0.048, 0.073]).

Additionally, the 'Social Avoidance' factor credibly predicted negative learning rates (mean = 0.023, 89% CrI [0.007, 0.040]) and learning rate difference (mean = -0.022, 89% CrI [-0.040, -0.005]) in opposite directions.
Specifically, individuals with higher scores on this 'Social Avoidance' factor learned more from negative social feedback, reflecting a negative learning bias.

No two-way interactions between condition and transdiagnostic factors were credible, nor did any other transdiagnostic factors show a credible association with computational learning parameters (all 89% credible intervals spanned zero), suggesting that the negative learning bias observed is specific to traits related to social avoidance and low social motivation.
We next sought to understand whether the three transdiagnostic factors moderated the effect of feedback valence on behavioral performance.
To do so, we fit a series of three-way mixedeffects regression models with transdiagnostic factors, learning rate parameters (𝛼 + and 𝛼 -), and valence conditions as predictors for task performance.

This revealed credible main effects towards choice accuracy (Figure 5a) for both 'Like' (posterior mean = 1.407, 89% CrI [1.227, 1.584]) and 'Dislike' conditions (mean = 1.097, 89% CrI [0.927, 1.270]), consistent with our repeated measures ANOVA analysis.
text.formatted: This revealed credible main effects towards choice accuracy (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5a</ref>) for both 'Like' (posterior mean = 1.407, 89% CrI [1.227, 1.584]) and 'Dislike' conditions (mean = 1.097, 89% CrI [0.927, 1.270]), consistent with our repeated measures ANOVA analysis.

text.text: We also observed a credible positive main effect of the positive learning rate (𝛼 + ; mean = 1.688, 89% CrI [0.021, 3.315]), alongside credible two-way interactions between the 'Like' (mean = -0.333, 89% CrI [-0.513, -0.152]) and 'Dislike' (mean = -0.222, 89% CrI [-0.390, -0.050]) conditions and 'Emotional Insensitivity', indicating that higher scores on this factor attenuated the benefits in accuracy typically observed in value-congruent learning contexts.

In addition, the negative learning rate (𝛼 -) showed credible positive interactions with both the 'Dislike' condition (mean = 1.138, 89% CrI [0.181, 2.102]) and 'Social Avoidance' (mean = 0.832, 89% CrI [0.094, 1.587]), such that faster learning from negative feedback was associated with higher accuracy in the Dislike condition and among individuals higher in Social Avoidance.
No three-way interactions were credible (all 89% credible intervals spanned zero).
Finally, we investigated whether transdiagnostic factors and learning rate parameters similarly influenced decision time (Figure 5b).
text.formatted: Finally, we investigated whether transdiagnostic factors and learning rate parameters similarly influenced decision time (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5b</ref>).

text.text: The 'Dislike' condition showed a credible main effect (posterior mean = -0.086, 89% CrI [-0.156, -0.016]) indicating faster decisions overall.

The negative learning rate parameter also showed a credible main effect (mean = 0.543, 89% CrI [0.246, 0.844]), two-way interaction with 'Social Avoidance' (mean = -0.359, 89% CrI [-0.702, -0.021]) and three-way interaction with the 'Like' condition and Social Avoidance (mean = 0.478, 89% CrI [0.148, 0.810]), suggesting that individuals with higher Social Avoidance scores and higher negative learning rates exhibited slower decision times specifically in the 'Like' condition.
The current study investigated how behavioral traits affect individuals' learning from social feedback utilizing a transdiagnostic approach and reinforcement learning.

Model comparison revealed that a simple reinforcement learning model with an initial value difference and separate learning rates for positive and negative feedback best quantifies the data, indicating asymmetric learning processes.
Learning rates were found to vary by task condition, with the positive learning rate higher in both valenced ('Like' and 'Dislike') conditions than in the 'Neutral' condition.
Individual differences in positive learning rates and positive learning bias were also both associated with higher choice accuracy in the 'Like' condition.
This suggests that individuals who learn more strongly from positive feedback make more accurate evaluative judgements in socially positive contexts.
Our factor analysis extracted three robust transdiagnostic dimensions: 'Social Avoidance', 'Emotional Insensitivity' and 'Depressive Self-Identity'.

These dimensions partly overlap with previous studies extracting transdiagnostic factors of psychopathology from general population samples (Gillan et al., 2016; Hoven et al., 2023; Oka et al., 2025).
text.formatted: These dimensions partly overlap with previous studies extracting transdiagnostic factors of psychopathology from general population samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Gillan et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Hoven et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Oka et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A previous study also previously labeled a 'Social Avoidance' factor strongly loaded items from measures of social anxiety, autism and apathy (Schafer & Schiller, 2025), and items for Depression and Borderline personality were found to load onto the same factor alternatively labelled 'Mood' (Schafer & Schiller, 2025).
text.formatted: A previous study also previously labeled a 'Social Avoidance' factor strongly loaded items from measures of social anxiety, autism and apathy <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Schafer & Schiller, 2025)</ref>, and items for Depression and Borderline personality were found to load onto the same factor alternatively labelled 'Mood' <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Schafer & Schiller, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: On-the-other-hand, the presence of an 'Emotional Insensitivity' factor not reported previously reflects the current study's specific focus towards assessing social evaluative learning.
Indeed, this factor loaded items from the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-10) and Apathy Motivation Index (AMI), questionnaires not included together in previous studies.
The extraction of this factor highlights the ability to understand and interpret the emotions of others as an important transdiagnostic dimension of social learning.
We further found significant associations between extracted transdiagnostic dimensions and task-related assessments of social evaluation learning.

Specifically, we show that a latent Social Avoidance dimension, cutting across social anxiety and related traits, is selectively associated with a negative learning bias and slower decision times towards positive social feedback.

This finding extends previous research using categorical assessments of social anxiety and BPD demonstrating similar learning biases using reinforcement learning models (Hoffmann et al., 2024; Koban et al., 2017 Koban et al., , 2023;; Korn et al., 2016) and increased deliberation in response to positive social information (Hunter et al., 2022; Van Der Molen et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This finding extends previous research using categorical assessments of social anxiety and BPD demonstrating similar learning biases using reinforcement learning models <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Hoffmann et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Koban et al., 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Koban et al., , 2023;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Korn et al., 2016)</ref> and increased deliberation in response to positive social information <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Hunter et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Van Der Molen et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The Social Avoidance factor further loaded items from the 'Social Motivation' subscale of the Apathy Motivation Index (AMI).

Though existing research on apathy has mainly focused on motivation control and effort-based decision-making (Costello et al., 2024; Derosiere et al., 2025), recent accounts have identified the motivation to socially engage as a key transdiagnostic measure given its comorbid presentation across multiple disorders (Barkus & Badcock, 2019) that may have distinct clinical and neurobiological correlates and respond differently to treatments (Chetcuti et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Though existing research on apathy has mainly focused on motivation control and effort-based decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Costello et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Derosiere et al., 2025)</ref>, recent accounts have identified the motivation to socially engage as a key transdiagnostic measure given its comorbid presentation across multiple disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Barkus & Badcock, 2019</ref>) that may have distinct clinical and neurobiological correlates and respond differently to treatments <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Chetcuti et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A second transdiagnostic factor, Emotional Insensitivity, reflecting lowered empathy and problems inferring the emotions of others, attenuated performance in both Like and Dislike conditions.

As empathy requires accurate emotional identification (Bird & Viding, 2014; Shamay-Tsoory & Hertz, 2022), individuals with reduced empathy are less capable of discerning changes in other's emotions (Coll et al., 2017; Gonzalez-Gadea et al., 2014).

text.text: This is commonly observed among individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) who show difficulties in social interactions (Bolis & Schilbach, 2017) due to challenges with understanding the intentions of others (Rosenthal et al., 2019).

text.text: In the current study, measures from the Autism Quotient (AQ-10) and 'Emotional Sensitivity' subscale of the Apathy Motivation Index (AMI) loaded strongly onto the Emotional Insensitivity factor, both of which may be obscured in categorical assessments or questionnaires.

Emotional apathy is robustly associated with prosocial behavior across different contexts (Contreras-Huerta et al., 2022), with higher levels predicting a lowered tendency to help others (Lockwood et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Emotional apathy is robustly associated with prosocial behavior across different contexts (Contreras-Huerta et al., 2022), with higher levels predicting a lowered tendency to help others <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Lockwood et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, few studies have specifically investigated its role with social reward learning.
In a study of dementia patients, those with high emotional apathy were found to demonstrate impaired learning towards social rewards (Wong et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In a study of dementia patients, those with high emotional apathy were found to demonstrate impaired learning towards social rewards <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Wong et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Our results further show that difficulties with interpreting the emotions of others directly impairs the ability to accurately evaluate social feedback.
The present study has some potential limitations.
Although we compared four RL models assessing selective learning from positive and negative feedback, along with an initialvalue bias, this represents a relatively restricted model space.

We deliberately adopted a parsimonious model specification without additional parameters (e.g., choice lapse, perseveration), because such parameters may only be informative in longer tasks or reversal-learning paradigms (e.g., Sugawara & Katahira, 2021), where lapses and choice-history effects are more readily dissociated from learning and decision noise.
text.formatted: We deliberately adopted a parsimonious model specification without additional parameters (e.g., choice lapse, perseveration), because such parameters may only be informative in longer tasks or reversal-learning paradigms (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Sugawara & Katahira, 2021)</ref>, where lapses and choice-history effects are more readily dissociated from learning and decision noise.

text.text: In the present task, however, there were no reversals and participants completed only 32 trials per condition block.
Given this limited number of observations, adding further parameters would risk weak identifiability and parameter trade-offs.
We also opted for not including an outcome sensitivity parameter, as outcomes in our task were binary rather than varying in their magnitude.

We therefore prioritized a simpler model that captured the core learning and choice processes supported by the task design and available data, though our winning model may nonetheless be regarded as best-fitting only among these candidate models.
Additionally, our sample is mainly comprised of females and consisted exclusively of university students.

This may explain the lack of any significant results with the Depressive Self-Identity factor, which strongly loaded items assessing depressive symptoms centred on guilt, lack of satisfaction and suicidal ideation.
The reported Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) scores in our sample (M = 12.52 ± 9.34) primarily reflect minimal (0-13) or mild (14-19) depression (Beck et al., 1996).
text.formatted: The reported Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) scores in our sample (M = 12.52 ± 9.34) primarily reflect minimal (0-13) or mild (14-19) depression <ref type="bibr">(Beck et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: However, depressive symptomatology may only emerge with more severe cases than those present in our non-clinical student population (Insel et al., 2010).
text.formatted: However, depressive symptomatology may only emerge with more severe cases than those present in our non-clinical student population <ref type="bibr">(Insel et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, given the non-clinical nature of the sample which consisted primarily of female university students, our findings should be interpreted as reflecting subclinical trait dimensions.
Further studies within clinical and more diverse samples are warranted before drawing conclusions about clinical mechanisms.

Future studies should therefore aim to capture a wider range of depressive symptoms across a more diverse sample (Geng et al., 2022), including recent approaches that take the advantage of large language models by simulating individuals with various personal profiles (Sohail & Zhang, 2025b; Li et al., 2026), both in laboratory and naturalistic conditions (Wang et al., 2026).

text.text: Taken together, combining a transdiagnostic measure of behavior with computational modelling, our study identifies key behavioral signatures of biased social evaluation learning.
Computational modelling revealed that participants exhibited asymmetric learning from positive versus negative social feedback, with learning rates varying by feedback valence.
A transdiagnostic factor reflecting social anxiety and motivational deficits biased social learning towards negatively salient information.
An 'Emotional Insensitivity' factor capturing difficulties in empathy and mentalizing was associated with sensitivity to positive social feedback.
These findings demonstrate how transdiagnostic traits influence social evaluative learning, identifying candidate computational processes that can be targeted in future studies.

The model space constituted four models: M1a (single learning rate, no initial-value bias), M1b (dual learning rate, no initial-value bias), M2a (single learning rate, with initial-value bias), and M2b (dual learning rate, with initial-value bias). (b) Next, we simulated 193 synthetic participants whose parameters were sampled using the hierarchical structure implemented in the Stan model.

Individual-level parameters 𝜙 𝑖 were generated using non-centered parameterization in probit-transformed space, then transformed to natural parameter bounds via effect coding and the cumulative normal distribution function, preserving the model's hierarchical structure and parameter constraints.

We repeated this procedure for all individual-level parameters of the winning model. (c) Then, we used the winning model as a generative tool to simulate behavioral data for our social evaluation learning task, namely, to simulate choices for 96 trials per participant (32 trials per condition).

Individuals' choices (denoted as D𝑖 ) were sampled from the sampling distribution conditional on individual-level parameters (𝜙 i ) from the previous step (i.e., likelihood function): 𝐷 𝑖 ∼ 𝑝(𝐷 𝑖 | 𝜙 𝑖 ) (9) (d) We fit the model to the simulated data ( D𝑖 ) in the same way as we did for the real data obtaining parameter estimates (i.e., posterior distributions) at both the group-level (e.g., μ 𝜑 , σ 𝜑 ) and the individual level (e.g., φ 𝑖 ). (e) Finally, we compared whether the posterior distributions recovered the true datagenerating parameters.

At the group level, we assessed whether the true parameter values fell within the 95% highest density interval (HDI) of the recovered posterior distributions for each iteration, and report coverage rates (percentage of iterations where true value falls within 95% HDI) across the 20 iterations (Supplementary Figure 1A).

To validate that the winning model could generate behavioral patterns consistent with the observed data, we conducted posterior predictive checks using a generative simulation approach.

We selected 4,000 posterior samples from the winning model's MCMC chains, where for each sample, we extracted the individual-level parameters (𝛼 + , 𝛼 -, 𝜏 ) for all 193 participants across all three conditions and used the model to simulate a complete synthetic dataset of 96 trials per participant (32 trials per condition), maintaining the same task structure and feedback contingencies as in the original experiment.
We then analysed each simulated dataset using the same statistical procedures applied to the observed data.

Doing so fully recovered the observed Like accuracy (observed = 68.7%, predicted = 70.4%, 95% HDI: 68.1%, 72.7%, Bayesian p-value = 0.133).

The remaining conditions were also well-recovered: Neutral (observed = 53.4%, predicted = 52.7%, 95% HDI: 50.5%, 55.0%, p = 0.585) and Dislike (observed = 68.5%, predicted = 68.5%, 95% HDI: 66.2%, 70.8%, p = 0.986), with all observed values falling within their respective 95% prediction intervals.

To check whether there was an initial bias in choice across conditions, we examined the first choice trial of each block (before any feedback had been received), and tested the proportion of participants choosing the positive word against chance (50%) with an exact binomial test, Bonferroni-corrected across the three blocks.

Across all three blocks, participants were significantly more likely to choose the positive word than the negative word (Neutral: 73.1%, p < 0.001; Like: 74.6%, p < 0.001; Dislike: 68.9%, p < 0.001; Supplementary Figure 3), indicating a consistent initial bias towards the positive option across all conditions before any learning had taken place.
